transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Desai (CTO - Apollo Robotics), Lina Park (ML Platform Lead), Carlos Vega (SRE)
Recording URL: (shared in Slack)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to reconcile cache hit-rate expectations, prefix key strategy, and tenant safety for a potential private deployment/pilot. Focus on throughput/latency tradeoffs, KV cache sharding, and how quantization and batching interact with hot-prefix behavior.

Topics covered:
- current Apollo traffic characteristics and hot-prefix skew
- proposed prefix-key hashing + tenant-aware namespacing
- impact of continuous batching on tail latency for small requests
- quantization profiles and cache compatibility
- VPC/on-prem constraints and KMS for cached payloads

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): okay hi everyone thanks for joining, uh we're on for about 50 minutes today. i'll let ravi drive the technicals, i'm here to take notes and follow up on next steps. samir, lina, carlos, you good with agenda?
[00:12] Samir: yeah thanks maya, quick yes, we mainly want to understand the model-level cache risks and how caching will affect our SLAs — especially the 95th percentile latency for short commands to the robot controller.
[00:23] Ravi (Redwood SE): cool, we'll start with a quick sketch of how our KV prefix cache slots map to worker pools then show some microbench numbers. fair warning some numbers are approximate, but we'll run the same profile on your samples.
[00:36] Lina: sounds good. also, uh, one ask — our SRE team needs to know about eviction policies, tenant isolation, and whether a misbehaving tenant can poison the cache.
[00:45] Carlos: and can we keep cached items encrypted at rest with our KMS? we have some constraints for log retention too.
[00:51] Ravi: yep, KMS and envelope encryption supported in Private deployment; caches are stored on local NVMe attached volumes in our runtime by default, we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; logs are configurable for retention.
[01:05] Maya: just to call out — SOC2 and ISO artifacts are in the doc pack we shared, i'll resend after this call.
[01:12] Speaker 1: okay thanks
[01:18] Ravi: all right so first slide — cache key strategy. we recommend a two-part key: tenant-id + prefix-signature. the prefix signature is a short stable hash of the first N tokens of the prompt; this is more deterministic than a whole prompt hash and allows prefix sharing.
[01:35] Samir: what's N typically? 32 tokens? 64?
[01:39] Ravi: yeah 32 is common but depends on your prompt templates; for us, 16–64 is the experimental sweet spot. smaller N increases collisions but improves hit rate when templates vary in suffix.
[01:50] Lina: collisions worry me — if two tenants have the same prefix signature, does that leak info or cause cross-tenant mixing?
[01:57] Ravi: critical point — tenant-id namespacing is mandatory in private/dedicated modes. prefix-signature collisions only affect within-tenant cache sharing; cross-tenant collisions are prevented by including tenant-id in the key. so there is no cross-tenant blend.
[02:12] Carlos: what about 'prefix morphing' — our prompts include dynamic IDs and timestamps, does Redwood recommend canonicalization?
[02:18] Ravi: yes canonicalization is key: strip volatile tokens, replace UUIDs/timestamps with placeholders before hashing; we can provide a small library you'll run to normalize prompts at the edge.
[02:27] Samir: okay that helps. show us numbers — how big of a hit-rate improvement do you see if we do prefix canonicalization?
[02:33] Ravi: on similar customers with templated prompts we've seen cold-hit to warm-hit conversions improving effective hit rate from ~12% to ~46% after canonicalization and hot-prefix pinning. but your distribution will matter.
[02:46] Lina: can you explain pinning?
[02:48] Ravi: pinning is marking a prefix signature as 'hot' and keeping it resident in the cache tier to avoid eviction. you can set a pin TTL and a max-resident count per tenant. pins are enforced per-tenant so one tenant can't pin everyone else's keys.
[03:03] Maya: quick question about eviction — what eviction policy do you use? lru? lfu? time-based?
[03:08] Ravi: default is a hybrid LRU-LFU with time-decay; we call it adaptive-evict. it favors frequently accessed prefixes but decays over time to adapt shifting workloads. we expose tuning knobs per-deployment.
[03:19] [03:25] Speaker 2: small note — the transcript may miss a few technical exact numbers
[03:28] Samir: that adaptive-evict sounds good, but our primary goal is to protect tail latency. if caching causes extra CPU overhead per request, it could regress our 95th.
[03:38] Ravi: yep, important tradeoff. for small requests we use a fast-path: check a fixed-size hash table in L1 in-memory, that adds ~0.3–0.6ms overhead on a warmed worker. the cache hit path saves 10s to 100s of ms on model inference depending on seq len. the miss path cost is slightly higher than no-cache due to the metadata ops but we can mitigate that with batching and async prefetch.
[03:58] Carlos: can you expand on async prefetch? that sounds helpful for our near-realtime controller commands.
[04:04] Ravi: prefetch is when we detect a likely next-prefix from conversation state and warm it in background; useful for predictable sequences. but for highly ad-hoc single-shot commands it's less effective.
[04:16] Lina: about batching, our controllers send many tiny prompts in bursts — will batching increase latency beyond acceptable?
[04:23] Ravi: continuous batching groups requests across concurrent connections up to a latency budget; you set the batch window (e.g., 5–20ms). for very low-latency needs you pick a small window 1–2ms but throughput suffers. we can show a plot: 5ms window gave 2.5x throughput with 1.2ms median added latency in one internal run.
[04:40] Samir: and quantization? does using 4-bit quantization change KV cacheability or correctness?
[04:45] Ravi: quantization is orthogonal to keying; cache entries store the model output tokens plus KV cache snapshot metadata. as long as the model family and quantization profile match, entries are valid. small numerical differences don't affect token-level outputs usually, but we always tie entries to a model-version+quant-profile tag. if you change quant config, those cached entries won't be used.
[05:06] Maya: note — for Dedicated and Private we allow multiple quant profiles, but rollout must be coordinated to avoid cache mismatch.
[05:13] Lina: what about cache-size accounting with quantized models — entries are smaller?
[05:17] Ravi: yes quant helps reduce runtime memory and cached payload size; in our internal tests switching from fp16 to 4-bit reduced KV snapshot size ~3.1x, increasing effective cache capacity similarly.
[05:27] Carlos: do you have a recommended per-tenant resident limit? we worry about noisy neighbors consuming all cache.
[05:33] Ravi: we typically recommend a soft quota per tenant plus a weighted eviction that biases toward smaller tenants if overall utilization spikes. you can enforce hard caps and a lease system for pins.
[05:44] Samir: can a tenant DOS the cache by generating many unique prefixes?
[05:48] Ravi: yes that's a vector; we mitigate via rate-limiting unique prefix creation, TTLs, and a prefix-entropy detector — it will mark a tenant's traffic as high-entropy and drop pining privileges until manual review or a cooldown.
[06:02] Lina: we liked the idea of an entropy detector, can you show what thresholds look like?
[06:07] Ravi: example rule: if >80% of requests from a tenant across a 10-minute window are unique prefix signatures, mark as high-entropy. thresholds are customer-tunable.
[06:17] [06:20] Speaker 3: oh sorry small crosstalk
[06:22] Samir: okay what about distributed cache coherence if we run two private nodes in different racks? do we sync KV snapshots?
[06:30] Ravi: we keep cache local to the worker for lowest latency; cross-node coherence uses async replication of 'pin' metadata only. we do not replicate full KV snapshots across nodes in real-time to avoid network cost. instead we rely on routing sticky sessions to the same worker group and on shared persistent cache for cold starts.
[06:47] Carlos: sticky routing — is that at session-level or prefix-level? how do you handle failover?
[06:53] Ravi: session-level sticky routing by default, with a fallback that routes to compatible model variant in other pools on failure. failover performs a cold fetch; we surface metrics so you can see the increased latency during failovers.
[07:05] Maya: quick interjection — we also provide per-prefix metrics in the Console so you can graph hot prefixes per-tenant and export CSVs for offline analysis.
[07:14] Lina: lovely. show us your benchmarking approach for measuring tail latency impact with/without cache.
[07:19] Ravi: we run three profiles: synthetic microbench with fixed token lengths; recorded production replay from customer traces; and mixed workload spike tests. importantly we measure 50/95/99 latencies and token-cost delta. we'll use your sample traces to run the recorded replay and share the raw CSVs.
[07:36] Samir: for the production replay, we want to preserve inter-request timing; do you support client-side replay harnesses?
[07:42] Ravi: yes we can ingest your trace (we asked for sample CSV) and replay with preserved timings; if you can't share raw logs we support an aggregated histogram or synthetic distribution.
[07:54] Carlos: about logs — we need PII redaction in traces and logs before you ingest them.
[08:00] Maya: understood, we can accept redacted traces or run the replay harness on-prem where data never leaves your VPC.
[08:07] Samir: good. can you summarize the expected 95th latency delta if we enable prefix caching for our short commands?
[08:15] Ravi: rough ballpark from similar workloads: enabling prefix caching with canonicalization and small batch windows gave 95th drop from ~220ms to ~95ms on a 512-token model workload, but again depends on your seq lengths and hot-prefix fraction. for tiny commands (<=32 tokens) the median was ~14ms and 95th ~28ms with cache; without cache median ~12ms and 95th ~70ms — so caching helps the tail but introduces a small median overhead.
[08:42] Lina: that last bit is important — i.e. small median overhead, but tail improves — exactly what we care about.
[08:48] Samir: any concerns about determinism of outputs when reusing KV snapshots? can it change randomness or sampling?
[08:55] Ravi: deterministic behavior is preserved for the same sampling seed/temperature; we tag cached entries with generation parameters. if you vary sampling parameters we won't reuse the entry.
[09:05] Carlos: network egress concerns: if cache warms with heavy model outputs, does that increase storage egress costs or cross-AZ traffic?
[09:12] Ravi: for Private deployment the cache is local NVMe so no cross-AZ egress for hit reads; replication is optional and can be disabled for egress-sensitive setups.
[09:22] Lina: let's talk about rollout strategy — we'll want to pilot on a single service first. recommended approach?
[09:27] Ravi: start with a shadow cache run: simulate cache checks but don't serve cached outputs, measure hit potential. then enable read-only cache (reads allowed but writes disabled), then enable full read/write with small pin quotas. we recommend 2-week pilot per service.
[09:41] Samir: can you do A/B by user cohort? we want to isolate effects on production.
[09:46] Ravi: yes A/B routing is supported in our rollout tooling; you can route a subset of tenants to cached path and compare.
[09:52] Maya: side note — our Console can export the per-route token-cost delta so you can bill back cost savings.
[09:58] Samir: great. any gotchas with on-prem where we can't use our KMS?
[10:03] Ravi: on-prem we support customer-managed KMS or a plaintext-disabled mode; we strongly discourage plaintext for cache material for security. if KMS unavailable we recommend deploying a thin KMS proxy or using an HSM connector.
[10:14] Carlos: we've got a hardware HSM, so that's fine.
[10:17] Lina: are there known interactions with quantization + batching that could cause tokenization drift?
[10:22] Ravi: tokenization is deterministic and unaffected by quantization; however lower-precision math can slightly change probabilities leading to different sampling outcomes. we surfacing those with quality-check alerts and you can tie evaluations to prompt sets.
[10:36] Samir: can Redwood run quality regression tests on our prompt set after a quant rollout?
[10:40] Ravi: yes, Redwood Optimize can run prompt-set evaluations and flag regressions against a baseline; we can include that in the pilot scope.
[10:47] Speaker 4: the timestamps are approximate in this transcript
[10:50] Lina: earlier you mentioned a small L1 hash check cost — can you break down resource overhead per worker? cpu and memory impact?
[10:58] Ravi: typical overhead per worker: ~150–250MB extra RAM for in-memory metadata and L1 hash table; CPU steady increase ~2–5% at typical request rates; for hot workloads it is amortized by lower model GPU utilization. we can give a rack-level sizing doc.
[11:14] Carlos: do you cap concurrent cache-check threads to avoid thundering herd?
[11:18] Ravi: yes we have semaphore-based concurrency for cache ops and adaptive backpressure on the serving runtime to avoid spikes.
[11:24] Samir: what's the observability surface we'll get during pilot?
[11:28] Maya: you'll get per-prefix metrics (hits/misses, avg latency), per-tenant quotas, eviction events, and lineage metadata indicating why a cache entry was invalidated.
[11:37] Lina: one last security question — are cache entries ever written to logs?
[11:41] Ravi: no, cached payloads are never logged in plaintext; we log only identifiers and metadata unless explicitly configured. logs are redaction-friendly.
[11:49] Samir: ok i think that covers the technical. quick recap pls?
[11:53] Maya: recap — 1) we'll run the recorded-replay benchmark on your sample traces (ravi) 2) send SOC2/KMS/Private deploy docs (maya) 3) carlos will send sample traffic and hot-prefix CSV 4) schedule on-prem proposal with infra team. agreed?
[12:08] Lina: yep
[12:09] Carlos: yep
[12:11] Samir: yep, thanks.
[12:13] Ravi: i'll add the benchmark plan to the follow-up email with the exact commands and expected CSV output.
[12:20] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with scheduling.
[52:00] End of recording
